case_study_insert.main_stem: Rowan & Jade Cooperative (RJC) is a fashion retail cooperative in the ethical clothing sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2011 by Aoife Rowan in Galway, the business sells recycled-fabric garments online and through two outlets, and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. RJC plans to invest $480,000 in a recycled-fabric clothing range and an e-commerce returns hub, financed by a $300,000 bank loan and $180,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.00 a unit and a selling price of $25.00, and sells 28,000 units a year. RJC faces two operational problems: fabric offcut waste has reached 7.4% and supplier deliveries are arriving late.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q4 2026: The Galway cutting room generated 7.4% fabric offcut waste by value, down from 9.1%, and 18 garments failed final inspection out of a batch of 1,200. Customer returns were 640 units and the complaint rate was 4.6% of orders. Average supplier delivery lead time lengthened to 12 days from 8 days. A survey of 500 members found 67% value recycled fabric and 62% would pay $2.00 more for it. Retraining one cutter in quality control costs $450, while a supplier quality assurance programme would cost $6,000 a year.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Rowan & Jade Cooperative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (January 2027): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.25% to 6.0%, raising the cost of variable-rate business borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage is set to increase 4.8% from $12.96 to $13.60 an hour from April 2027, pushing up labour costs in retail and fulfilment. (3) Organic cotton and recycled-fabric input costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year, while consumer spending on ethical clothing grew 1.8% over the same period.

questions.question_text: RJC plans to finance its $480,000 recycled-fabric range with a $300,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for RJC of using $180,000 retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Applying $180,000 of retained profit to the $480,000 range means RJC borrows less and avoids interest and capital repayments on that portion, protecting cash flow alongside fixed costs of $210,000 a year. The money saved can be spent on tackling the 7.4% offcut waste or on the $6,000 quality assurance programme, rather than being paid to a lender, and the $25.00 selling price need not be raised to cover finance costs.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no security or repossession risk, so the new e-commerce returns hub is safe even if demand for recycled fabric disappoints. It also preserves member control of the cooperative: no bank can attach conditions to how the $300,000 is used, so the democratic leadership can respond to the 67% of members who value recycled fabric and the 62% who would pay $2.00 more. Retaining the $180,000 also demonstrates financial strength when negotiating with suppliers whose deliveries currently take 12 days.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to RJC's funding decision and expansion.

questions.question_text: RJC is launching its new recycled-fabric clothing range. Consider local newspaper advertising, social media advertising, or in-store demonstrations at its two outlets. Which should RJC choose to promote the range? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local newspaper advertising: Print ads can reach Galway shoppers cheaply and suit a cooperative's community image, with simple delivery before the launch. However, RJC sells online as well as through two outlets and needs volume close to 28,000 units a year, so a regional newspaper has limited reach and cannot show the texture and colour of recycled fabric that 67% of members value.

Social media advertising: Visual platforms can demonstrate recycled garments, target ethical-fashion audiences nationally, and link directly to the website and the new e-commerce returns hub. Spend is measurable within the $480,000 budget and can highlight the premium that 62% of members would pay. The drawback is that feeds are crowded, costs can rise, and results depend on creating strong images of the fabric.

In-store demonstrations: Demonstrations at the two outlets let customers touch the fabric and ask staff questions, which could reduce the 4.6% complaint rate and the 640 returns. They also build member loyalty. However, they reach only shoppers near the outlets, are labour-intensive for a workforce of 52, and do little to drive the online sales that the returns hub is meant to serve.

Recommendation: RJC should choose social media advertising, supported by small in-store demonstrations. Social media gives national, measurable reach at controllable cost and can carry the recycled-fabric and $2.00-premium message to the 62% of members willing to pay more; in-store events alone are too local and costly per customer, and newspapers are rejected as static and regionally limited. Demonstrations can be retained as a low-cost supplement at the two outlets once online demand is established.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of RJC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of RJC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why newspapers and demonstrations lose.

questions.question_text: RJC's fabric offcut waste has reached 7.4% and supplier deliveries are late. Explain two benefits for RJC of using democratic leadership in its flat structure.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the workforce of 52 to propose ways of cutting the 7.4% offcut waste, and the flat structure means a cutter's suggestion reaches Aoife Rowan without passing through several management layers. This is practical knowledge from the Galway cutting room, where 18 garments failed inspection out of 1,200, so small changes suggested by operators can quickly reduce the gap from the earlier 9.1% waste figure.

Point 2: Consultation increases commitment to quality, which supports the $6,000 quality assurance programme and makes staff more willing to accept retraining at $450 per cutter. Lower waste protects the $25.00 selling price and the contribution earned on 28,000 units, helping RJC cover fixed costs of $210,000 a year and the $480,000 range investment. Democratic discussion with members also builds trust when the cooperative must decide how to handle supplier lead times that have stretched from 8 to 12 days. Member consultation also fits the cooperative ownership structure, so changes to cutting routines are more likely to be accepted by the 52 employees in the Galway operation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RJC's waste, leadership and structure.

questions.question_text: RJC wants to reduce its 7.4% fabric waste and late supplier deliveries. Consider retraining cutters in quality control or introducing a supplier quality assurance programme. Which should RJC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Retraining cutters in quality control: At $450 per cutter this is cheap against the $480,000 investment, and it addresses waste directly in the Galway cutting room where 7.4% of fabric is currently lost and 18 of 1,200 garments failed inspection. Staff learn to spot faults before cloth is cut, and training can be spread across the workforce of 52. Its limit is that it cannot fix late deliveries or poor fabric arriving from suppliers, so the 12-day lead time would remain.

Supplier quality assurance programme: Costing $6,000 a year, this sets standards with suppliers and checks material before it reaches the cutting room, so it tackles both the incoming cause of the 7.4% waste and the late deliveries that have stretched lead times from 8 to 12 days. It may need staff time to audit suppliers and will not immediately improve the 18 failed garments if cutting skills are weak, but it prevents problems earlier in the chain.

Decision: RJC should introduce the supplier quality assurance programme first, with limited cutter retraining alongside it. The $6,000 annual cost is small beside fixed costs of $210,000 and the $480,000 range, and it attacks the external causes — late and variable fabric — that training alone cannot reach; retraining is therefore rejected as the sole response because it leaves the 12-day lead time untouched. A few $450 training places should still be funded so the 18 inspection failures fall, combining the two approaches rather than relying only on in-house fixes. The cooperative should review the 7.4% waste figure and the 12-day lead time each quarter so it can judge whether the $6,000 annual spend is delivering value.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two quality approaches with limited application to RJC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of RJC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of RJC with a well-justified decision covering cost, waste and supplier lead time.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RJC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $210,000 ÷ ($25.00 − $11.00) = $210,000 ÷ $14.00 = 15,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 15,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $25.00 − $11.00 = $14.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $14.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RJC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even output of 15,000 units against sales of 28,000 units leaves a margin of safety of 13,000 units, showing the cooperative can absorb a demand fall while repaying the $300,000 bank loan.
2. Contribution per unit of $14.00 allows managers to test the $2.00 premium that 62% of members would accept: a price of $27.00 would raise contribution to $16.00 and speed repayment of the $480,000 range cost.
3. The break-even figure sets a sales target for the new e-commerce returns hub and helps judge whether the $6,000 quality assurance programme is affordable from contribution above 15,000 units.
4. Unit cost of $18.50 ($210,000 ÷ 28,000 units = $7.50 plus $11.00 variable cost) gives a benchmark to track the 7.4% offcut waste each quarter and check whether the $450 retraining is working.

questions.model_answer: (i) break-even output = 15,000 units | (ii) contribution per unit = $14.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 13,000 units against 28,000-unit sales; testing the $2.00 premium on $14.00 contribution; covering the $300,000 bank loan and $6,000 quality programme; unit cost of $18.50 to monitor 7.4% waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RJC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has RJC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.25 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.40 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.90 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $80,000 + $85,000 + $35,000 = $200,000; 2025 current assets = $75,000 + $95,000 + $40,000 = $210,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $160,000 in 2024 and $150,000 in 2025 gives the first pair of figures. Removing stock leaves $120,000 in 2024 and $135,000 in 2025, which divided by the same liabilities gives the second pair.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The first ratio rose from 1.25 to 1.40 because current assets grew by $10,000 while current liabilities fell by $10,000, giving more cover for the $480,000 range commitments. The second ratio improved from 0.75 to 0.90, so RJC is less dependent on selling its $75,000 of inventories to pay short-term debts, which matters when 7.4% offcut waste and 12-day supplier lead times can make stock hard to move. However, trade receivables rose from $85,000 to $95,000, tying up cash needed for the $6,000 quality assurance programme, and a $300,000 bank loan still creates interest obligations if rates rise.

Conclusion: RJC's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher, and the rise in the second measure shows the gain is not just due to inventory. The main residual concern is slower collection from customers, so the cooperative should tighten credit control before borrowing further for the returns hub. The partners should also monitor the $40,000 cash balance, because the $480,000 range and the 12-day supplier lead time can both create sudden calls on liquidity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether RJC's position improved.

questions.question_text: RJC is considering charging a $2.00 premium for its recycled-fabric range. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RJC of this decision.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey shows 62% of members would pay $2.00 more for recycled fabric and 67% value it, so the premium is supported by evidence and would lift contribution per unit from $14.00 to $16.00. Across 28,000 units that would generate $56,000 a year (28,000 × $2.00), helping RJC cover fixed costs of $210,000 and part of the $480,000 range investment despite a 1.8% rise in ethical-clothing spending.

Disadvantage: Charging more may put off the 38% of members who would not pay the premium, and the 11.2% rise in organic cotton and recycled-fabric costs could mean the $2.00 is needed just to protect the existing $14.00 contribution rather than add profit. With offcut waste at 7.4% and 640 returns already logged, a higher price could make customers less tolerant of faults, raising complaints above the current 4.6% of orders. RJC should therefore test the premium on a limited batch before committing the whole range.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RJC's survey, costs and waste.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 6.0%, the 4.8% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in organic cotton and recycled-fabric costs will affect RJC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): If RJC's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost increases by 0.75% of $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). This is small next to fixed costs of $210,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed there is no immediate extra charge. The cooperative can limit the risk by fixing the rate, so this is the least pressing of the three changes.

Minimum wage rise (4.8%, to $13.60 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 52 but no hours worked or pay rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. Qualitatively, the rise increases the cost of running the two outlets and the returns hub and cannot be avoided. Because 7.4% of fabric is wasted and a $450 cutter retraining place is budgeted, any wage increase that is not matched by productivity will raise unit cost and narrow the $14.00 contribution, but the effect is spread across the cooperative rather than concentrated on one input.

Input cost inflation (11.2%): The insert gives a $11.00 variable cost per unit but does not decompose it. If all of it rose by 11.2%, the increase would be 0.112 × $11.00 = $1.23 per unit, and at 28,000 units that is $34,440 a year (28,000 × $1.23). Even a smaller rise would erode the $14.00 contribution on every garment sold; the $2.00 premium that 62% of members would accept can offset only part of it.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in fabric costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 28,000 units, reaches a larger annual sum than the $2,250 interest change, and directly threatens the contribution that funds the $480,000 range. The interest rise is modest and can be fixed, and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert, so both rank lower; RJC should negotiate bulk fabric prices and introduce the premium gradually while monitoring the 7.4% waste figure.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to RJC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on RJC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of RJC with a well-justified judgement that fabric cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
